Neutron-star cooling: how much do pairing gaps, envelope and mass move the curves?

Working report, 19 November 2026. 67 runs of the neutron-star-cooling solver, compared with the ns-thermal-catalogue review values of the same date.

The five reference cooling curves used in the catalogue differed from each other by up to a factor of ten at 1–30 kyr. This sweep shows that the difference comes mainly from the pairing gaps and the envelope, not from the equation of state. It also gives a minimal-cooling band against which the observed sources can be tested.

Main results

Without direct Urca, the core neutron-triplet gap is the dominant choice, followed by the core proton gap and the envelope composition. EOS and mass shift the curves by at most about 0.5 dex.

The lower edge of the minimal-cooling band is robust. It is the same within 0.06 dex across 11 published triplet gap models.

Against that band, PSR J0007+7303 is the only source that is clearly too cold: at least 1.1 dex below. Vela Jr and J0205+6449 are marginally below (about 0.2 dex). B1727−47 is below only if its envelope is iron.

1. What was run

All runs use the solver as published: mesh C, initial redshifted temperature 1010 K, B = 0, the Yakovlev et al. (2001) modified Urca rates and BCF2024 bremsstrahlung. Each run stops when Lγ∞ falls below 1030 erg/s. The crust neutron gap is fixed to the default (model 7), because the solver’s own earlier scan showed it changes L by at most 6%.

Direct Urca opens at 1.15 M☉ for BSk22, 1.60 for BSk24, 1.63 for BSk25 and 1.98 for APR, and never for BSk26, whose maximum mass is 2.17 M☉. Throughout, “minimal cooling” means every run below its EOS threshold.

Each run took 19–51 s on one core, about 35 minutes in total. Every run closed its energy balance; the largest error was 1.5% against a 2% tolerance, and the median was 0.02%. Per-run details are in tables/run_qc.csv.

2. Pairing gaps and envelope in a single star

The proton gap sets the overall level. A strong proton gap suppresses modified Urca throughout the core and raises L by about a factor of 4 at 104 yr (log L 33.93 compared with 33.33 with no proton gap). The weak AO proton gap is close to having no gap at all.

The triplet gap sets the drops. Each sharp fall in panel (a) is the onset of pair-breaking emission, when the core temperature falls below the critical temperature of the triplet gap. With the high-Tc AO gap this happens before 300 yr. With the low BEEHS gap it happens near 103 yr without proton pairing, but only at 1–3 × 104 yr with a strong proton gap. That interaction is why gap channels cannot be scanned one at a time. Once their drop has happened, all combinations with a triplet gap lie within about 0.3 dex of each other (log L 32.4–32.7 at 3 × 104 yr).

This also explains the original five reference curves. With the default deep triplet gap, the critical temperature reached inside the star depends on the central density. It is 0.41 × 109 K in BSk24 but 0.92 × 109 K in APR, so the drop happens at about 3 × 104 yr in one and about 300 yr in the other. The apparent EOS dependence was really a gap-placement effect.

The envelope effect reverses with age (panel b). An accreted (light-element) envelope has a higher surface temperature for the same base temperature. It is therefore 0.5–0.8 dex brighter while the star is cooled mainly by neutrinos, but it then cools faster once photons dominate. The crossover is near 105 yr for weakly paired stars and near 2 × 104 yr for strongly paired ones, whose heat capacity is small. The extreme case, strong proton plus high triplet gap with an accreted envelope, falls below 1030 erg/s by 80 kyr. The run with the original default gaps reproduces the existing BSk24 reference curve within 0.07 dex.

3. Mass and equation of state

Without direct Urca, EOS and mass matter little (solid lines). In the cold setting, every star without direct Urca lies within about 0.1 dex up to 104 yr. In the hot setting the two heaviest stars without direct Urca, BSk26 at 2.1 M☉ and APR at 1.7 M☉, form a second family about 0.4 dex lower. The strong proton gap only extends to kF ≈ 1.3 fm−1, so their dense centres keep unsuppressed modified Urca.

With direct Urca, “hot” and “cold” swap. The proton gap does not reach the dense centre where direct Urca operates, but the high triplet gap does, and suppresses it there. So in heavy stars the nominally hot setting (dashed lines in a) is the colder of the two. For example, BSk24 at 1.7 M☉ has log L 30.99 at 104 yr in the hot setting and 31.90 in the cold one. With no gaps at all, BSk22 at 1.4 M☉ falls below 1030 erg/s by 22 kyr.

The transition is sharp. BSk24 gives log L 32.70 at 1.55 M☉ and 31.5–32.0 at 1.65 M☉, a change of about 1 dex for 0.1 M☉. In practice there is no lower floor once direct Urca is allowed: some heavy, weakly paired star can always explain a cold source. The physically informative comparison is therefore with the minimal-cooling band.

4. How robust is the cold edge?

The cold edge comes from one gap model, so it was tested against ten alternatives. AO stays the coldest from 3 × 103 yr onwards. Before that, HGA12-deep is lower by only 0.06 dex. So the cold edge is essentially independent of which published triplet gap is assumed.

A larger gap does not give a colder star. The Baldo model (peak Tc 5.4 × 109 K) pairs the whole core so early that the pair-breaking emission is over before the ages that matter, and then suppressed. The coldest models are those whose pair-breaking emission is strongest at the relevant ages, here AO and TToa.

At the other extreme, EEHOr (peak Tc 0.17 × 109 K) is barely active and stays near the hot reference until about 105 yr. Most of the width of the minimal-cooling band therefore comes from a single microphysical uncertainty: the strength and density profile of the core neutron-triplet gap.

5. The bands compared with the sources

A source counts as below the band only if its whole error box lies below the band at every age in its range. Upper limits are treated as boxes extending to zero luminosity.

PSR B1727−47 (upper limit)40–80 × 103below by ≥ 0.31 dexinside

Cas A, Crab (upper limit), IC 443, Vela, S147, Monogem, B1951+32 (upper limit), J0357, five XINS—insideinside

J0007+7303 is the robust case. Even if its luminosity ceiling were 2–3 times higher, which is plausible given the spectral model, it would still lie at least about 0.6 dex below the band. That requires enhanced cooling, for example direct Urca in a heavier star.

Vela Jr and J0205+6449 are marginal. They are about 0.2 dex below, which is within their distance and emitting-component systematics. For J0205 the lower part of the box comes from a small-area hot-spot fit, which is not a measurement of cooling luminosity.

B1727−47 depends on the envelope. With an accreted envelope, the strongly paired cold edge drops fast enough after 3 × 104 yr to reach its upper limit.

B2334+61 depends on the distance branch. It is inside the band with the current hybrid box, which pairs the near-distance age with the far-distance luminosity. On the self-consistent near-distance branch (about 7.7 kyr) it would be 0.8–1.3 dex below: 0.8 dex with the whole-surface atmosphere fit that is valid near 1 kpc, more with the hot-spot interpretation. On the far branch its age is unknown but probably older, and it would be inside. This is the first source to discuss next.

No source is above the band. Cas A is inside it, but at ages where several triplet gap models produce their pair-breaking drop (Figure 3), so it is the source most sensitive to that choice. S147, the most luminous source near 30 kyr, sits well inside the band, about 0.8 dex below the Fe hot edge.

6. Reference models

ReferenceDefinitionHow closely it follows the band edge
Cold (minimal cooling)Strong proton gap (HGA12≈CCDK) + AO triplet gap; BSk26, 2.1 M☉; Fe envelope. For the light-element case, the accreted version is colder after about 2 × 104 yr.Within 0.18 dex of the Fe lower edge at all ages (rms 0.06 dex); stable across 11 triplet models
Hot (minimal cooling)Strong proton gap, no triplet gap; BSk26, 1.7 M☉. Accreted envelope up to about 1.5 × 105 yr, Fe afterwards.Within 0.49 dex as a single Fe run (rms 0.38). Only the composite follows the hot edge at all ages.

The two references differ essentially in one choice: whether the core neutrons pair into a triplet state with a gap large enough to trigger pair-breaking emission at the relevant ages. Neither was tuned to the observed sources.

7. Limitations

  • Only three proton gap options were sampled. The triplet gap was tested broadly (11 models), but at one mass and with one proton gap.
  • The magnetic field is zero. Only fully iron and fully accreted envelopes were run, with no partially accreted cases.
  • The solver’s documented approximations remain: the pair-breaking response, the APR crust composition, and the BSk25 and BSk26 table rows omitted by the reader. Spatial convergence was not re-tested; only mesh C was used.
  • Comparisons below 1030 erg/s, after about 1 Myr, are not possible with these runs.
  • The source boxes are the catalogue’s current working values. Their own open issues (hot-spot versus whole-surface components, distance branches) are discussed in the catalogue audit and affect the verdicts above.

Contents of this folder

  • report.html: this report, with the figures embedded.
  • figures/: the four figures as separate PNG files.
  • tables/run_table.csv: one row per run, giving its settings, direct-Urca flag, log L at eight ages and final age.
  • tables/cooling_sweep_curves.csv: all 67 cooling curves, in the same format as cooling_five_eos.csv in the catalogue.
  • tables/bands.csv: the upper and lower edges of the three bands on a common age grid.
  • tables/run_qc.csv: runtime and energy-closure error per run.
  • tables/source_verdicts.txt: the source comparison.
  • tables/plan.csv: the run plan.
  • runs_inputs/: the 67 solver input files.
  • scripts/: plan, runner, analysis and plotting scripts. These expect the solver repository next to the sweep folder.
